Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Vignette:
Kai is a 22-year-old UX designer who lives alone in a small apartment in a city he moved to only a year ago. He came to therapy at the urging of his supervisor, who noticed that Kai had become increasingly withdrawn at work, often flinching when colleagues approached his desk from behind, and that he had started taking his lunch breaks alone in a stairwell rather than in the shared kitchen. Kai agreed to come because he was tired of feeling exhausted and strange, and because he had begun to wonder if something was genuinely wrong with him.

The event that changed everything happened two years ago, when Kai was still living with his family in a coastal town in the Philippines. A typhoon struck without warning during the night. The storm surge flooded their ground-floor home so quickly that Kai and his parents had to climb onto the roof. He remembers the taste of salt water and diesel fuel mixing in his mouth as waves broke over him, forcing him to swallow and spit and swallow again. He held onto a piece of the roof that had torn loose, his neck craned at an unnatural angle as he tried to keep his head above the water. His father’s hand slipped from his own at one point, and Kai spent what felt like hours screaming into the wind before his father surfaced again, gasping. They were rescued at dawn, but the taste of that water never fully left him. Even now, months and years later, there are moments when he is brushing his teeth or drinking a glass of tap water and the flavor returns, metallic and oily, and his throat closes. Sometimes the emotion of that night floods him without any image at all — he will be sitting at his desk, designing a wireframe, and suddenly his chest is tight and his eyes are wet, and he has no idea why, only that he is terrified and alone and the world feels like it is ending.

In the months after the typhoon, Kai’s family relocated to Manila. He threw himself into finishing his degree online, then took a job offer in the United States. He told himself he was starting over. But the move only deepened a feeling that had already taken root: that he no longer belonged anywhere. The disaster had erased the home he knew, and the new country felt alien. He began to distrust the people around him. Colleagues seemed friendly, but Kai was certain they were not what they appeared. He watched for signs of falseness — a smile that dropped too quickly, a compliment that felt rehearsed. He started to believe that everyone was hiding something, that no one could be relied upon. The isolation grew quietly. He stopped messaging his old friends from Manila because he could not explain what he was feeling, and he did not make new ones. He ate dinner alone every night, and on weekends he stayed in his apartment, scrolling through design blogs or staring at the wall.

The neck pain that began during the typhoon never really went away. It had become a constant, low-grade ache that flared when he was stressed or tired. But it was more than a physical sensation. When his neck tightened, Kai felt physically unwell — a wave of nausea, a sense of dread, as if his body was remembering the strain of holding himself above the water. He began to avoid anything that reminded him of the typhoon: news about storms, documentaries about natural disasters, even the sound of heavy rain. But the triggers were not always external. Sometimes a wave of nausea would hit him in a meeting, or his neck would lock up while he was cooking, and he would have to sit down and breathe slowly until the feeling passed. He had come to believe that he was fundamentally different from other people, that he was set apart by something invisible and permanent. He did not know how to explain it, and he was afraid that if he tried, no one would understand.

What finally brought Kai to seek help was a moment at work three weeks ago. His supervisor asked him to join a team brainstorming session in a conference room with a large window overlooking the parking lot. It began to rain, hard and sudden. Kai felt the taste of salt water in his mouth. His neck seized. He stood up without a word, walked out, and locked himself in a bathroom stall for forty minutes. When he came out, his supervisor was waiting in the hallway. She asked if he was okay. Kai said yes, but she did not look convinced. She gave him the name of a therapist and said she would support whatever he needed. Kai took the card, not because he believed therapy would help, but because he was afraid that if he did not try something, he would lose his job, and then he would have nowhere left to go. He is not sure what he hopes for, exactly. Mostly, he is afraid that the therapist will confirm what he already suspects: that he is broken in a way that cannot be fixed, and that the taste of that water will never wash out.
